The growth calculation discards negative deltas instead of clamping the aggregate growth, contradicting its documented evidence semantics and potentially producing unsupported risk recommendations.

Pure telemetry attribution over supplied records; commands and paths are classified as strings and never executed, opened, rendered, or transmitted.
Compliance numerators, denominators, contributing-session counts, null handling, and tier-0 correlational provenance are explicitly computed and reproducible from tool-call fields.
Evaluation is bounded by supplied sections, signatures, sessions, and calls; the only repeated per-session native-tool aggregation is linear over each session plus one global pass.
Privacy assertions verify that section prose and a sentinel secret are absent from emitted records; fixtures perform no filesystem or network operations.
Tests cover section boundaries, stable identifiers, content-change hashes, typed reference extraction, fence exclusion, sorting, mtimes, and nullish inputs.
Unit-test code is not a production hot path or shipped runtime surface.
The parser is pure, excludes body prose from output, strips fenced examples from reference extraction, and neither accesses files nor renders/transmits parsed Markdown.
Section IDs, hashes, headings, mtimes, and typed references are deterministically derived from the supplied artifact, with documented handling of collisions and malformed fences.
Parsing and extraction are linear passes over each supplied document with output limited to structural records and deduplicated references.
Filesystem writes are confined to fresh OS temporary directories with locally constructed filenames; no untrusted path is executed or written.
Tests reproduce empty, malformed, partial, retry, SDK-attribution, TTFB percentile, byte-cap, and directory-filtering behavior from explicit log artifacts.
Unit-test fixtures are not a production hot path or shipped runtime surface.
The server-only scanner performs no writes or egress, filters directory entries to .txt files, checks targets are regular files, and returns only derived metrics rather than ~/.claude log content.
TTFB samples cite paired request/chunk timestamps; retry, stall, and SDK signals come from explicit log patterns, with malformed and incomplete samples excluded.

Directory entry and per-file byte limits are optional and default to effectively unlimited values, allowing synchronous ingestion and full-string splitting of every debug log without a default budget.

findings.title: Compaction drops do not reduce the reported rolling growth rate
findings.where: src/lib/parse-compaction-risk.ts:61-65 documents that an in-window compaction pulls growth down, but src/lib/parse-compaction-risk.ts:123-130 sums only positive adjacent deltas; src/lib/parse-compaction-risk.ts:255-262 turns that value into recommendation text.
findings.what: For a context series such as 100k → 120k → 20k → 40k, the implementation reports (20k + 0 + 20k) / 3 = 13.3k tokens/turn. The documented net-delta interpretation would clamp (40k - 100k) / 3 to zero. The inflated value can add growth risk points and emit a 'steady growth' recommendation immediately after a compaction, so the claim is not reproducible from the stated calculation semantics.
findings.fix: Compute the signed aggregate delta across the selected window and clamp the final average to zero, or explicitly redefine the field and recommendation as average positive-only expansion and remove the claim that compactions pull it down. Add a compaction-in-window regression test.
findings.acceptance: A regression fixture containing 100k → 120k → 20k → 40k produces contextGrowthRate=0 under the documented net-growth semantics and emits no growth-threshold suggestion; monotonic-growth fixtures retain the expected arithmetic.
findings.verifyNote: Adversarial re-read confirmed that line 126 conditionally adds only d > 0 while lines 63-65 and 117 state that negative growth is clamped and a compaction pulls the signal down; scoring and recommendation branches consume the inflated result unchanged.

findings.title: Debug-log ingestion has no default entry or byte budget
findings.where: src/lib/parse-debug.ts:226-258 scans files synchronously; src/lib/parse-debug.ts:232-237 maps an omitted or invalid maxFileBytes to -1, disabling the size check; src/lib/parse-debug.ts:140 splits each complete file string into another line array.
findings.what: With default options, every discovered .txt file is synchronously read in full and then duplicated into a split-line array, while all TTFB samples are retained and sorted. The entry helper also receives an effectively unbounded default. A large or accumulated ~/.claude/debug directory can therefore block ingestion and create memory proportional to total log volume, with no shipped default budget or probe.
findings.fix: Define finite default maxEntries and maxFileBytes budgets, skip oversized files before reading, and parse files incrementally or line-by-line so the full text and split array are not simultaneously retained. Record skipped-file/byte counts for observability.
findings.acceptance: Calling parseDebugDir(dir) without options enforces documented finite entry and per-file byte limits; an oversized fixture is skipped before read/parse, bounded-memory ingestion is demonstrated, and metrics expose or log the number of files skipped by budget.
findings.verifyNote: Adversarial re-read confirmed both limits are optional, omitted maxFileBytes becomes -1, the scanner calls readFileSync for each accepted file, and parseDebugLog immediately materializes text.split('\n'); no default byte budget or ingestion probe exists in the audited implementation.
